articles.title: Kennedy Center chair fired by Trump buys Blue sculpture recently torn down by president: report
articles.summary: Trump ousted major arts donor David Rubenstein in 2025 as the president pushed to rename the venue after himself
articles.body:
The former chair of the Kennedy Center, who was ousted from the institution's board by President Donald Trump last year, has reportedly purchased a beloved blue sculpture that was removed from the venue's grounds last week.

Billionaire philanthropist David Rubenstein has purchased Joel Shapiro's towering stick-figure sculpture Blue from the foundation dedicated to the artist, according to The New York Times.

The 24-foot-tall sculpture, which was abruptly dismantled and removed from the grounds of the Trump-dominated Kennedy Center last week, is reportedly set to be installed at the Sculpture Garden of the National Gallery of Art.

Last year, Trump fired Rubenstein , a major arts donor and co-founder of private equity firm The Carlyle Group, only to install himself as the Kennedy Center's "amazing" new board chairman. Trump said he removed Rubenstein from the position because he did not share the president's "Vision for a Golden Age in Arts and Culture," Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.

The president also appointed loyalists to fill out the board in a bid to rename the venue after himself and close the building for renovations as he speeds through multi-million construction projects throughout Washington, D.C.

The Independent has requested comment from a representative for Rubenstein and the National Gallery of Art.

Shapiro's site-specific Blue sculpture, installed in 2019, depicts an electric blue stick figure in mid-kick in a "celebration of possibility," according to the artist . Shapiro died last year.

The Kennedy Center made no advance announcement of the removal plans. The National Park Service only posted a street closure notice earlier last week indicating that a teardown project was set to begin before dawn and be completed by 1 p.m.

Workers began removing the piece before sunrise.

"We are deeply grateful to Joel Shapiro for the years Blue has spent animating our campus and connecting visitors to his vision," a Kennedy Center spokesperson told The Independent as workers were disassembling the piece.

"We are honored to have been stewards of his vibrant work and a part of his enduring legacy," the spokesperson said.

According to the Kennedy Center, the artwork was removed at the request of the Kennedy Center and the Joel Shapiro and Ellen Phelan Foundation. A representative for the foundation declined to comment to The Independent at the time.

Advocacy group Hands Off the Arts, which has campaigned against Trump-led changes to the institution, told fans of the piece to "say your final goodbyes."

"Wednesday, September 2, 2026 will forever be known as the day the United States government tore down a piece of public art at the behest of a petulant crybaby," the group wrote on Instagram. "But it won't be the last."

Shapiro's piece was "designed specifically as a joyful and welcoming feature for the public grounds of the expansion," the group said.

Last month, the board voted to install Trump's name on the building's white marble facade — again — despite court orders that have prevented the president from making any attempt to rename the landmark after himself.

Under a resolution approved by the board, the words "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump" will appear under President John F. Kennedy's name, and the phrase "Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund" will also be added once an endowment — also in Trump's name — reaches $100 million.

Together, those changes could mean that the building will be named: "The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump endowed by The Trump Kennedy Center Fund."

The board also voted to name the grounds where the building stands after Trump.

Under the resolution, that space will be called "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."

Trump's name was removed from the building this summer after U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper ruled that Congress made it "crystal clear" that the memorial is only to be named after the assassinated former president, "and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial" based on Trump's "unilateral say-so."

Scaffolding and a massive white tarp that were erected to strip the metal nameplates from the facade are still standing outside the building.

Only "The John F." and part of the letter "K" are currently visible.

Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, who is leading the legal battle against the Trump-led changes, filed an emergency motion last month asking Cooper to block the board's latest vote, which her legal team called a "breathtaking act of defiance" of the court's order.

The Department of Justice has argued that the venue will rapidly deteriorate without the support of the president, whom government lawyers have called the "sole hope" for its financial and structural survival.

Justice Department officials also said the building could be demolished in the future if the court stops the Kennedy Center's two-year closure, renovation and re-branding plan.

"In plain English, Defendants have not-so-subtly said: 'What a nice Kennedy Center you have here. What a shame should something happen to it,'" lawyers for Beatty wrote in court filings last month . "This is a breathtaking assault on the rule of law. It is delusional. And it must stop."

articles.title: Ohio Democrat Amy Acton reflects on a ‘rough day’ as witnesses recall ‘frightening’ confrontation
articles.summary: Democrat Amy Acton vowed to continue on as a “fierce warrior” in her campaign for Ohio governor Monday, a day after law enforcement officials said an armed man aggressively attempted to confront her at a county fair.
articles.body: Democrat Amy Acton vowed to continue on as a “fierce warrior” in her campaign for Ohio governor Monday, a day after law enforcement officials said an armed man aggressively attempted to confront her at a county fair. “Yes, we had a rough day yesterday,” Acton told the crowd at a Labor Day parade and festival in Cleveland, NBC affiliate WKYC reported. “I am a fierce warrior in this fight. That’s exactly why I’m running. I refuse to look the other way like people didn’t look the other way when I was a struggling kid in Youngstown, Ohio. I won’t look the other way, and you are refusing to look the other way.” Acton was not injured during the Sunday incident at Mahoning County’s Canfield Fair, near Youngstown, but several others in the crowd were, officials and witnesses said. A suspect, Patrick Havas, was arrested on charges of disorderly conduct and assault. Havas, 38, could be formally charged as soon as Tuesday, said Gerry Ricciutti, a spokesperson for the Mahoning County sheriff and prosecutor. On Sunday, Havas approached the local Democratic Party’s tent, where Acton was speaking, and began pushing his way through the crowd, according to accounts from the Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office and the Ohio State Highway Patrol. Havas “knocked multiple fairgoers over” while advancing toward Acton, according to the Highway Patrol, which provides a security detail to Acton because of her candidacy for governor. A statement from Acton’s campaign spokesperson, Addie Bullock, said the suspect “lunged” at her. Law enforcement officials reported finding two handguns, a set of brass knuckles and a Taser on Havas after arresting him. He did not brandish the weapons during the incident, according to the Sheriff’s Office. Officials have not yet offered their thoughts on what motivated the confrontation. Acton faces Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in the November election. Polls have shown a close race in a state that has become redder since the political rise of President Donald Trump, an early backer of Ramaswamy’s campaign. On Monday, three witnesses to the incident told NBC News that they saw the suspect knock two older attendees to the ground. They also said they watched as Acton, a physician and former state health director, administered care to them. “Amy immediately went into action and gave care … while emts made it to the scene,” Lindsay Yaggi, referring to emergency medical technicians, wrote in a Facebook message. “She apologized that this happened to them and made sure they were ok before they had her leave.” In an interview, former Rep. John Boccieri, D-Ohio, said he was standing “within arm’s length” of Acton and that the suspect made it “within feet” of her. The suspect entered the tent and appeared to be attempting to ask Acton questions while filming the confrontation on his cellphone, he said. “He was yelling, ‘Dr. Acton! Dr. Acton!’ And when the State Highway Patrol and the security detail grabbed him, he said, ‘I was just trying to ask a question,’” said Boccieri, who described the incident as “an aggressive move from a very large man.” The suspect “started rushing and barreling towards Dr. Acton.” Boccieri added: “He was not coming in the tent to give Dr. Action a hug. He was coming in more aggressively, and that’s what I saw.” An older male attendee who was knocked down in the pursuit fell face down in the mud “right in front of Dr. Acton,” Boccieri recalled observing. “She immediately began rendering aid and care to the man.” Acton, 60, served as Ohio’s health director under term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, during the early days of the Covid pandemic. Her role issuing stay-at-home orders made her a target for conservative activists and protesters, some of whom reportedly wielded guns and signs bearing antisemitic messages outside the Statehouse in Columbus and outside her home. Acton, who is Jewish, downplayed those incidents as a factor in her resignation in June 2020. Ramaswamy, 41, has emphasized Acton’s work during the pandemic in the general election contest. His campaign and his allies also are attacking Acton’s character — attempting to frame her as a quitter and calling attention to a 2019 incident at Acton’s home that police described as a “domestic dispute.” No charges were filed. “Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence,” Connie Luck, a Ramaswamy campaign spokesperson, said in a statement Sunday. “What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope that no one was hurt.” The Canfield Fair, which is celebrating its 180th year, is an annual destination for politicians in the Youngstown area, which like Ohio has moved more to the right in recent years. Trump and then-Vice President Joe Biden both visited in 2016. “This is the largest county fair in Ohio,” Boccieri said. “Thousands of people come here, and to know and understand that someone’s walking around with a gun and brass knuckles and rushing towards a gubernatorial candidate is just frightening and scary. Luckily, the security detail was able to prevent something more tragic.”

articles.title: Trump posts updates about his DC ‘beautification’ projects
articles.summary: President Donald Trump made several posts on social media on Monday morning with pictures of statues and landmarks around Washington, D.C., that the National Park Service has been updating. Trump has been emphasizing his efforts to “beautify” D.C., including constructing an arch in his honor, fixing fountains and gold-plating statues, among other projects. Each post…
articles.body:
President Donald Trump made several posts on social media on Monday morning with pictures of statues and landmarks around Washington, D.C., that the National Park Service has been updating. Trump has been emphasizing his efforts to “beautify” D.C., including constructing an arch in his honor, fixing fountains and gold-plating statues, among other projects.

Each post contained photos of a project around the city and a status update about the project from Greg Wischer from the Department of the Interior.

One was of the George Mason Memorial fountain , which, Wischer said, as quoted by Trump, had been repaired for the first time in eight years. Photos in another post showed water flowing at fountains at the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial.

Several posts featured statues that had been cleaned and waxed, including statues of Dante Alighieri and Joan of Arc in Meridian Hill Park.

The Department of the Interior under Trump has already restored some high-profile fountains around D.C., including at Meridian Hill Park and Union Station.

Trump still has a long list of projects that are part of his campaign to “Make DC Safe and Beautiful Again,” including his controversial White House ballroom and triumphal arch. The president has also sought to repaint the Reflecting Pool, which he posted recently was soon to be reopened after months of controversy over the renovations.

articles.title: One year into free child care in New Mexico, too many kids and not enough slots
articles.summary: SANTA FE - A year after New Mexico launched free child care for all families, Dakota Rivera still can’t find a place to send her kids. The mom of two was ecs...
articles.body:
One year into free child care in New Mexico, too many kids and not enough slots

SANTA FE - A year after New Mexico launched free child care for all families, Dakota Rivera still can't find a place to send her kids.

The mom of two was ecstatic when the state's Democratic governor, Michelle Lujan Grisham, announced last September that New Mexico would expand its day care assistance program to any family who wanted it.

But Rivera lives in a city with an acute shortage of child care centers. She still spends her days piecing together care with help from family members, canvassing social media and searching for babysitters.

"I think the systems that they put in are great, sure, but it's just not there yet," Rivera said, as she tried to answer work emails while holding her 8-month-old daughter, who was cooing and waving a plastic giraffe. "In five years, maybe. For parents trying to do it now, it's impossible."

When Lujan Grisham first announced the program in a state with a majority-female legislature, it was widely praised as a historic step to address an issue that consumes the lives of parents everywhere - and their incomes. Costs for caring for an infant can often exceed a year's rent, according to the U.S. Department of Labor.

But the groundbreaking program, in part funded by the state's sizable oil and gas revenue, has had a rocky debut.

The number of children who have enrolled has skyrocketed, far outpacing the capacity of day care centers in the state. Lujan Grisham has had to grapple with legal challenges, including a whistleblower case from the program's chief financial officer, who says she was fired after flagging an $83 million budget deficit.

Critics have raised concerns that annual costs could balloon to more than $800 million - nearly $400 million more than when the program debuted. State legislative analysts have also found that newly eligible, higher-income families may be squeezing out some of the lowest-income recipients. The state's GOP leaders dubbed the program "Nannies for Millionaires."

The stakes could not be higher as more Americans say raising children is too expensive and as political leaders look to New Mexico as they try to address overwhelming child care needs. Vermont and Connecticut already have smaller-scale programs, and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) is rolling out free day care for thousands of the city's 2-year-olds - a move that has also had a bumpy start.

Sara Mickelson, an early-childhood policy expert and former deputy Cabinet secretary for New Mexico's Early Childhood Education and Care Department (ECECD), said the state got two big things right when rolling out its plan: the money and the vision. But a subsidy doesn't help parents if there is no program to take it, she said.

"Families there are still calling around and finding no openings," she said.

Lujan Grisham has acknowledged the challenges, telling MSNBC, "We're building a rocket ship as we fly it." The governor said in an interview with The Washington Post that she sees the plan as a "game changer" for her state and a blueprint for the rest of America.

She said the program would need more than $1 billion from the state's early-childhood fund over the next five years, $300 million more than the legislature initially allocated.

"No one said it was an inexpensive enterprise, and likely it shouldn't be," she said. "It should be something that invests in child well-being and development, and that's what we're doing."

A report Tuesday from ECECD touted its successes, citing "dramatic gains" in child care enrollment, growth in higher-quality care and wages for workers topping $19 an hour, $3 more than the national median.

"We've stabilized and really strengthened the child care sector in New Mexico in ways that are critical. It's critical that families have choices, and these choices reflect the kind of care they need," said Elizabeth Groginsky, the ECECD Cabinet secretary. But, she said, "there's more work to be done."

The move to universal child care was the culmination of a decade-long journey for advocates in New Mexico, a poor, majority-minority state of 2 million whose fourth-graders rank last in both reading and math, according to the biennial National Assessment of Educational Progress, the "nation's report card."

In 2020, the state legislature created a trust fund with about $300 million in oil and gas revenue to support early-childhood education and care, a pot that has since ballooned to about $11 billion.

New Mexico expanded income limits for the child care assistance program three times. In 2022, more middle-class families became eligible in a change that allowed 80 percent of families in the state to participate.

Last September, Lujan Grisham took the final step, announcing that New Mexico would be the first to open its subsidized day care to any family, a move estimated to save families $13,000 a year per child.

"That was always the vision," she said at the time. "It took us this long to realize it, but by golly, we did."

The announcement was met with applause and cheers, but behind the scenes, state legislators - who said they had not been informed that the program would become universal - were confounded, along with some members of the department's own staff.

"We were all shocked," said state Sen. George Muñoz, a Democrat and chairman of the Senate Finance Committee. "Nobody knew about it until the day it was in the paper. All of a sudden we were all calling each other, saying, 'Where did this come from?' 'Did anybody from the governor's office talk to you about it?' Nope, we were all in the dark."

Word of the expansion moved quickly through the young moms groups of Santa Fe, a picturesque city that is not always easy on parents with its high cost of living and long waiting lists for day care that can stretch for years.

Meghan Montelibano Gorman, 33, a mother of two and a marketing consultant who runs an Instagram account called "Santa Fam," moved with her husband back to Santa Fe in 2022 from Denver to be closer to family.

She initially tried to work full time doing marketing for the Santa Fe New Mexican newspaper. But managing a full-time job and the health of her older son Charlie, who has breathing and speech issues, quickly took a toll. She recalled acing a presentation one day, but the elation she felt was sliced with guilt because she had to move Charlie's speech therapy to do it. Even if they had been able to get a spot for day care, it would have gobbled up most of her $35,000 annual salary.

"It was untenable," she said. "Something had to give and it was me. I broke through that process."

With the support of her husband, an engineer, she left her job to start her own marketing company. Creating her own flexible hours, she cared for her son and second child, Max, now 2, with help from family members.

She said her life changed for the better when they were able to enroll both kids in universal day care this summer before Charlie moved into prekindergarten. She was able to pay off Charlie's medical bills and triple her income.

"I was in shock this was happening," she said of the new state program. "Happy, of course, ecstatic. I had been so in the trenches - with the scheduling, the negotiations, wiggling into shapes I didn't fit into to make our life fit - this felt too good to be true."

Now, she said, "I've reclaimed some of my joy because I'm not stressing out all the time." She later invited program organizers to her Santa Fam parent meetup to help spread the word.

Enrollment has soared to 47,000 from 32,000 since the launch, but so have the costs.

In February, the legislature passed a bill formalizing the program. Only afterward did lawmakers learn from the Lujan Grisham administration that it already faced a $60 million budget shortfall, Muñoz said.

The legislature's finance committee said in a report last year that the program could soon cost the state almost $849 million annually, a roughly $400 million increase from the fiscal year 2026 payouts. The governor disputed that finding, saying that the legislature's analysts did not factor in those who would remain in private care.

Ismael Torres, the committee's chief economist, warned in a committee hearing last month that such a spike could put the trust fund that helps pay for the program in jeopardy.

Jacob Candelaria, a former Democratic state senator, is representing two former New Mexico Early Childhood Education and Care Department staffers who said they were penalized after raising red flags about the finances. He also represented a trio of Republicans who challenged the program in court and lost.

He said Lujan Grisham, who is term-limited and will leave office this year, has embraced universal child care as her legacy issue and a "stepping stone" to the national stage in 2028. She was eyed as a potential running mate for both former president Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, and this year successfully pushed to have New Mexico become the fourth state to vote in the 2028 presidential primary - a prime slot.

"Whatever the governor has planned for the next steps of her career, this universal child care narrative is a central piece of it," Candelaria said. "My clients have had the unfortunate luck of getting in the way."

The governor said she expects the whistleblower lawsuits to fail like the GOP suit did. She also expects the issue of child care to be a topic during the presidential debates in 2028, she said.

"You're going to have this as a signature issue about where the country goes," the governor said. "We need a universal approach supporting families who need care."

Asked whether she expected to be on the presidential stage herself, she said, "I hope I'm in the ears of people on the stages, because I know we need this."

The state has worked to address the capacity issues by offering low-interest loans to providers and attempting to speed up approvals. New Mexico was short an estimated 15,000 day care slots when the program was launched and added 6,700 since then, an ECECD spokesman said.

Anne Liley, the director of the First Presbyterian Child Development Center in Santa Fe, said the majority of families at the center now use the universal system instead of paying privately. Most are families with two working parents whose incomes are just above the previous limit of $106,600.

"It's been huge for them," she said. "When both people are working, trying to get by, and you have two children, half your income is going to child care."

More than 400 children are on her center's waiting list, so she's looking for a new space that would allow her to add about 85 infants and toddlers, a critical need. She's still trying to find the right building, which is difficult in Santa Fe with its many historical structures, she said.

Critics ha8ve said allowing families who made more than $106,600 (for a family of three) last year to use the universal system has squeezed out low-income families who desperately need care. Sometimes, they are seasonal workers who leave and then return, only to find a wealthier family has taken their slot, analysts said.

The program serves 3,700 families who make above that amount, according to the ECECD report this month.

"If you're making that kind of money, you really don't need this," said state Rep. Mark Duncan, a Republican. "Are we keeping kids who really need it out because they didn't get there first? That's my concern."

Lujan Grisham said they did away with income requirements because the state is "building for an equitable system."

"You don't make it for poor people, you don't make it for middle class and you don't make it for billionaires, you make it for everybody," she said. "We're really leaning into the developmental well-being aspect and family stability."

When James Krantz, a tech executive, and his wife Caitlin, who owns a marketing company, had their son a little over a year ago, they too found lengthy day care waiting lists in Santa Fe. He said the state is now paying for their babysitter after the couple made the argument that "universal child care" should include private in-home care.

"Doesn't universal apply to everybody?" he asked. Having the full-time sitter has been "magical" for the couple, who can work with somebody "to closely align with how we want to raise our child."

Muñoz said that going forward the department needs to focus its efforts on "at-risk kids, low-income kids and special-needs children … to really deliver on the transformational investment the state is making."

When Rivera, 29, a legal assistant, gave birth to her son three years ago, she looked at the cost of day care and was "stunned" by the price tag - more than $20,000 a year. She and her husband, a technician, cobbled together a complicated schedule: She does her work from home, and other family members are enlisted to help. She makes an online calendar to keep everyone on task.

"I'm constantly overwhelmed by the process," she said. "My kids are seventh-generation New Mexicans. To feel like we're not welcome anywhere when the family has been here so long is so frustrating."

She and her husband have completely "lost hope" on finding help for this school year and are looking to 2027 for relief. Maybe she can find a preschool for her son and a day care for her daughter then.

articles.title: Rudy Giuliani urges Mamdani to not attend 9/11 anniversary
articles.summary: Rudy Giuliani, the former mayor of New York City who later worked as President Trump’s personal lawyer, publicly criticized current Mayor Zohran Mamdani for planning to attend a 9/11 commemoration ceremony at Ground Zero on Friday. “Frankly, whatever he’d like to say, he doesn’t agree that September 11th was an Islamic terrorist attack on the…
articles.body:
Rudy Giuliani, the former mayor of New York City who later worked as President Trump’s personal lawyer, publicly criticized current Mayor Zohran Mamdani for planning to attend a 9/11 commemoration ceremony at Ground Zero on Friday.

“Frankly, whatever he’d like to say, he doesn’t agree that September 11th was an Islamic terrorist attack on the United States of America,” Giuliani said in an interview with Newsmax on Sunday. “Having lost friends there, and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he’s coming.”

Giuliani led the city through the aftermath of 9/11 as mayor. Now, he has taken to espousing conspiracy theories about Muslims and Mamdani. He is the most prominent of a series of conservatives who have called on Mamdani not to attend the ceremony, including in a petition with 100,000 signatures that cites the mayor’s support for people who are viewed as being “dismissive of American institutions or insufficiently critical of extremist ideologies.”

Giuliani’s criticism was heavily tinged with anti-Muslim sentiment and false claims about Mamdani’s beliefs.

“They have every desire to take us over. This is not, they want to be just another religion, they want to dominate us,” Giuliani said of Muslims. “Mamdani is a clear supporter of that.”

Mamdani has already responded to an online petition that wanted to ban him from attending the ceremony. He also signed two executive orders last week related to 9/11, one to overhaul the city’s emergency preparedness plans and one to establish the day as a “Citywide Day of Remembrance and Service.”

“I will proudly honor the families, the survivors, the first responders forever impacted by that horrific terror attack by standing alongside them at this year’s 9/11 commemoration, reaffirming that we will never forget the solemn day felt by all of us who call this city home and, frankly, by all of us who call this country home,” Mamdani said in July.

Mamdani will be with four of the five living presidents at Ground Zero, and Vice President Vance. Trump will be at the ceremony at the Pentagon, another site of the 9/11 attacks, where he will give a speech.

articles.title: Smotrich calls for expulsion of UK ambassador after 'Post' report of planned settlement trade ban
articles.summary: National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also responded to the reports of the settlement trade ban by calling for Israel to recognize the Falkland Islands...
articles.body:
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich calls for the expulsion of the UK ambassador to Israel over reports of a settlement trade ban, accusing the UK of being conquered by radical Islam and attacking Jews and Israel.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir responds to the UK's settlement trade ban by calling for Israel to recognize the Falkland Islands as Argentine territory under occupation, accusing the British of stealing money from the Argentine people.

The UK is likely to announce a ban on trade with Israeli settlements following a debate on Jewish safety in Parliament, with measures expected to include a ban on settlement goods and targeted sanctions on British institutions and individuals.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also responded to the reports of the settlement trade ban by calling for Israel to recognize the Falkland Islands as "Argentine territory under occupation."

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the United Kingdom's ambassador to Israel to be ejected from the country on Monday night, following reports that the UK was planning to announce a ban on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday.

"Expel the British ambassador tonight!" Smotrich posted on X/Twitter. "The British Mandate in the Land of Israel is over."

Smotrich added that Israel would not be "a doormat trampled by an antisemitic government," and called the UK " a country conquered by radical Islam , trying to save itself from economic and social decline by attacking Jews and the State of Israel."

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also responded to the reports of the UK's settlement trade ban by calling for Israel to recognize the Falkland Islands as "Argentine territory under occupation."

According to Ben-Gvir, "The British are not content with merely occupying the territory; they also carry out oil drilling there and steal the money from the Argentine people."

He also called upon Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to recognize Argentina's sovereignty over the islands, and to impose sanctions on Britain "as long as the occupation continues."

UK likely to announce ban following debate on Jewish safety

Earlier on Monday, sources told The Jerusalem Post about the UK's plan to announce the ban on trade with settlements .

Candidatos à eleição são proibidos de distribuir camisetas, bonés, chaveiros, canetas ou qualquer outra coisa que possa proporcionar um presente ao eleitor.

Além de não poder oferecer brindes, tem uma situação ainda mais grave: oferecer alguma vantagem em troca do voto .

E a punição não vale só para quem tenta comprar o voto. Quem pede ou aceita uma vantagem para votar em determinado candidato também pode responder pelo crime . A pena pode chegar a quatro anos de prisão, além de multa.

Ou seja, você não deve aceitar dinheiro, cesta básica, nem combustível, por exemplo. E a regra também vale, mesmo que o presente não seja um bem material. Uma consulta médica, uma cirurgia ou até a promessa de um emprego também podem entrar na lista de proibidos.

Casos assim, podem ficar configurados o crime de corrupção eleitoral. E nem é preciso que a troca chegue a acontecer.

Pelo código eleitoral, dar, oferecer ou até prometer uma vantagem com essa finalidade pode configurar crime, mesmo que a oferta não seja aceita.

articles.title: IAEA warns over Iran nuclear access as Western powers push UN referral
articles.summary: UN nuclear watchdog urges Iran to cooperate, as Western powers push to refer its nuclear file to the Security Council.
articles.body:
France, Germany, the UK, and the US are urging the IAEA to report Iran to the UN Security Council due to the nuclear watchdog's inability to verify Tehran's nuclear material for over a year.

IAEA chief Rafael Grossi stated that Iran has not provided information on its declared nuclear material or facilities, leading to inspectors being unable to conduct on-site verification, raising proliferation concerns that need urgent rectification.

Iran has rejected the move, claiming its nuclear program is peaceful, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei arguing that restrictions on inspectors are a result of US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities, warning of necessary measures if the Western powers pursue the resolution.

France, Germany, the UK and the US are pressing the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to report Iran to the UN Security Council, as the nuclear watchdog warns that it remains unable to verify Tehran's nuclear material more than a year after losing access to key facilities.

IAEA chief Rafael Grossi told the agency's Board of Governors on Monday that Tehran had provided no information during the latest reporting period on the status of its declared nuclear material or facilities, and inspectors had been unable to conduct on-site verification.

"It is more than a year since the Agency lost continuity of knowledge" over previously declared stocks of uranium enriched to as much as 60 percent at facilities hit in US and Israeli attacks in June 2025, Grossi said.

He described the lack of information and access as a proliferation concern that "needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency", calling on Iran to restore effective cooperation with the IAEA.

The nuclear watchdog's warning comes as the four Western powers seek support for a draft resolution at the 35-member board that would send the Iran issue back to the UN Security Council (UNSC) for the first time in two decades, according to Reuters.

The proposed text asks Grossi to transmit the resolution, previous board decisions and his latest report to the UNSC and General Assembly. It also calls on Iran to provide the information and access required by inspectors.

Iran has rejected the move and maintains that its nuclear programme is peaceful.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Western governments were again turning to the IAEA after failing to achieve their objectives elsewhere.

"Whenever they run out of options, they turn to the agency and Grossi," Baghaei said at his weekly news conference on Monday.

He argued that restrictions facing inspectors were a consequence of US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities and that it was unreasonable for those governments to blame Tehran for the resulting loss of access.

Baghaei warned that Iran would take "necessary measures" if the Western powers pursued the resolution.

The draft has not yet been formally submitted to the board, and negotiations over its wording are continuing. Even if it is approved, any concrete action at the Security Council could face opposition from Russia and China, two of the five permanent veto powers.

articles.body:
An emergency crew rescued a construction worker from high up in scaffolding on the White House North Portico on Monday afternoon, responding to a dispatch saying that a worker had been injured.

The worker was put into a stretcher and ambulance, which then went to the hospital, according to the Washington Post . The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the worker’s condition, the Post said.

Workers have been removing scaffolding and draping around the portico that were up for renovations to the columns and entrance that started in July. The scaffolding is now being removed in preparation for Chinese President Xi Jinping to visit the White House on Sept. 24.

The North Portico project is one of many Trump has started, or mused about, around the White House grounds. A renovation of the driveway to add a helipad was completed this week.

articles.title: Trump calls for a Bombardier plane ban, drawing pushback from a GOP senator
articles.summary: President Donald Trump asserted Monday that the Canadian aerospace company Bombardier should no longer be allowed to sell its planes in the U.S., opening a new front in his trade war with Canada.
articles.body: President Donald Trump asserted Monday that the Canadian aerospace company Bombardier should no longer be allowed to sell its planes in the U.S., opening a new front in his trade war with Canada. The move drew an objection hours later from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., whose state hosts Bombardier’s U.S. headquarters. It’s the latest example of pushback from Republican senators against Trump’s Canada trade policy, which has sparked back-and-forth tariffs months from the midterm elections. “NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!” Trump wrote in a Monday post on Truth Social. “Their products aren’t good enough!” Trump further charged that the company depends on “American Buyers, American Companies, American Airports, and American Service — All while Canada blocks our GREAT American Banks, and Companies, throughout the U.S.A.” “If they want our Market,” Trump added, “they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank.’” The president’s missive drew a response from Bombardier, which defended its investments in the U.S., and from Moran, who in a post on X noted that the company is a major employer in his state. “The presence of Bombardier in Wichita supports a local workforce of more than a thousand employees, who contribute their talent and expertise to our nation’s defense and aerospace capabilities,” Moran wrote. “This afternoon, I reached out to the Trump administration to make certain the President is aware of the significant contributions of Bombardier to Kansas and the importance of its presence in Wichita to many Kansas workers at Bombardier and in the Bombardier supply chain,” Moran added. In a Monday statement, Bombardier described itself as “a strong contributor” to the American aerospace industry that is responsible for “creating tens of thousands of jobs across the United States.” “Bombardier’s American workers are based all around the United States with sites in Kansas, Texas, Arizona, Florida, Connecticut, Illinois, Delaware, California, Washington D.C. and New Jersey, as well as overall direct employment presence in more than 20 states,” the company said. Bombardier also noted a robust U.S. supply chain, as well as the “American-made components” used in their planes. “Significantly, the wings for the world’s fastest business jet are made by American workers at Bombardier’s facility in Red Oak, Texas while crucial flight control components are made in Bombardier’s Los Angeles, California area facility,” the company added. “Bombardier has also announced extensive plans to grow its defense activities as well as its service network and will, later this year, inaugurate a new facility in Fort Wayne, Indiana.” Trump’s clash with the company comes amid a trade war in which the president has imposed new tariffs on Canadian products and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America. Canada responded to Trump’s tariffs by announcing retaliatory tariffs on nearly $20 billion worth of goods. Those tariffs are expected to take effect Tuesday.

articles.title: Russia launches deadly strikes on Kyiv as pause during US envoy visits ends
articles.summary: US envoy says ‘encouraged’ by talks as White House official told Reuters next steps to be announced in coming weeks.
articles.body:
Russia has struck Kyiv after a three-day pause in attacks on the Ukrainian and Russian capitals expired, following a visit by two US envoys that yielded no tangible progress towards peace.

At least two were killed in the air raids, and seven wounded, according to the Kyiv city military administration.

Two residential buildings were damaged by Russian air raids early on Tuesday, city officials in Kyiv said. Drones hit buildings in the capital city as well as in the Boryspil and Fastiv districts on the outskirts of Kyiv, according to the State Emergency Service of Ukraine.

An air raid alert, published by the Kyiv city military administration, urged residents to take shelter due to the threat of an “enemy” drone attack.

Following the reported attacks in Ukraine, Russian regional Governor Roman Busargin said a Ukrainian drone attack injured several people after hitting civilian infrastructure in Saratov, nearly 1000km (621 miles) from Moscow. The number of causalities remains unconfirmed.

Russia and Ukraine pledged to halt strikes on each other’s capitals for three days as Washington dispatched envoys to Moscow and Kyiv. However, fighting continued elsewhere.

Attacks paused after leaders Vladimir Putin of Russia and Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine announced the ceasefire during the visits by US President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, to Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.

Russia’s state news agency TASS confirmed that the three-day suspension Putin had ordered for his forces expired on Monday evening local time.

Witkoff and Kushner held talks with officials in Moscow and Kyiv regarding ending the conflict. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov called the more than three-hour meeting in Moscow on Saturday “highly useful”.

After talks with Ukraine’s Zelenskyy, Witkoff said : “We’ve had a very meaningful discussion, substantive, important, and we are very encouraged, and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes.”

Witkoff also raised the prospects of reviving three-way negotiations to end the war.

A White House official told the Reuters news agency that the next steps regarding the war, which Russia began with a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022, would be announced in the coming weeks.

articles.title: What College GameDay Taught Us About Welcoming Opposing Views
articles.summary: "Sports debate has always been at its best when it challenges its audience to think, question and engage. Saturday provided an opportunity to do exactly that...
articles.body:
It's not the first time, nor will it be the last. This past Saturday, College GameDay devoted a segment to the upcoming vote on the Protect College Sports Act this week in Congress. Regardless of your political leanings, a college football pregame show devoted time at the official kickoff of the season to publicly support national legislation with no representation of the opposing view.

Is this the new normal? Is this the expectation moving forward? Without question, college football needs some sort of reform. But is this act the fix? And should it be debated on a college football pregame show to kick off a new season of Saturdays in the fall? If Saturday was an example, where was the debate? There was none.

I'm not naive enough to believe sports and politics have never mixed on sports television programming. I've always argued that if there is a direct connection between sports and a political debate, then engage. But engage properly. Except, Saturday provided a moment where the intersection was direct. However, the forum was not open to the other side.

Instead, this was lobbying. Not discussion. This was advocacy, not debate.

Yes, Nick Saban is a staunch supporter of the act proposed in Congress. In fact, he testified before a Senate committee in support of the bill and appears in a commercial supporting it. Yes, Pat McAfee is also a supporter of the act. He's said as much on his daily sports talk program.

But the heart of the legislation is still up for debate. The vote comes this week. Saban himself said he considers the bill 80% good.

Why only 80%? Where is the other 20% lacking? That could have used another point of view from someone opposed to the act.

Make no mistake about it. ESPN has been a lightning rod for years over talent embracing social commentary and political conversation on air. The network has faced criticism from both sides of the political spectrum when its talent has ventured into broader discussions involving sports and politics.

We've seen it with Colin Kaepernick and the national anthem debate. We've seen it in discussions surrounding the NBA and WNBA with issues of political and social policy. Depending on the audience and the topic, ESPN has always been accused of being too "this" or too "that."

But at the heart of those criticisms is often the same complaint: the absence of an opposing viewpoint. Taking a stance instead of embracing debate and conversation. That doesn't mean every argument needs to receive equal weight. What it does mean is that when a program chooses to enter a discussion involving a matter of public policy, the audience deserves an opportunity to hear more than one perspective.

If shows or talent wish to dive into these discussions, they should ensure that both sides have representation. That's what fair coverage deserves, and what every sports talent should understand.

At the end of the day, every program should give viewers and listeners an informed and entertaining point of view. Political discussions demand that broadcasters present more than one perspective. Any sort of reform has its supporters and detractors. News networks attempt to provide both sides. Talk radio also makes an effort to present both angles of a discussion.

Without debate, nothing is accomplished. Compromise is never reached. Agreement is never final.

There is a dissenting side to the legislation in Congress. But you wouldn't know that by watching College GameDay on Saturday. Withholding that point of view when you choose to enter the discussion is misguided. It doesn't accomplish the service your program is designed to provide: entertain and inform.

Saturday's edition of College GameDay should be an example every sports talk program attempts to avoid. If a program chooses to enter the political arena, it has a responsibility to do more than present one side of the argument. When legislation is being debated, especially legislation that could directly impact the sports being discussed, the audience deserves to hear the strongest arguments from both supporters and opponents. It didn't happen.

By doing so, that's giving viewers and listeners enough perspective to form their own opinions. Isn't that the goal? Have the audience decide?

Talent can have a position. Programs can have a point of view. But when the discussion involves politics and public policy, presenting only one side risks turning commentary into advocacy. And that distinction matters.

Sports debate has always been at its best when it challenges its audience to think, question and engage. Saturday provided an opportunity to do exactly that and missed it. The Protect College Sports Act deserved a conversation, not a campaign pitch.

Every sports talk program entering similar territory should remember the difference.

articles.title: Massachusetts late-term abortion extremism can be help Republicans in the midterms
articles.summary: Democrats are aggressively promoting legal abortion through all nine months. Pro-life Republicans must highlight this.
articles.body:
Massachusetts Democrats recently made a huge moral and political blunder with national implications. They just don’t know it yet. It is up to Republicans whether they will use the great gift of contrast to their advantage.

Last month, Gov. Maura Healey (D) signed an expansion of the Bay State’s abortion law, which already allowed abortions for any reason up to six months, with exemptions thereafter. The new law allows abortion through all nine months of pregnancy, up to the moment, of birth based on the “professional judgment” of the abortionist who profits, which cannot be questioned or reviewed.

With the stroke of a pen, they joined the shameful company of only seven other nations worldwide , including Communist China.

Disturbingly, Healey and the group of lawmakers surrounding her celebrated with evident glee. The scene recalled New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo (D) seven years earlier, lighting up One World Trade Center upon stripping all protections for unborn children out of his state’s law s .

People who rarely or never comment on abortion are expressing new shock and revulsion. At SBA Pro-Life America, as our team visits millions of homes across America, we routinely speak with horrified voters who had no idea how extreme our laws have gotten.

As summer ends, I have written to Republican candidates nationwide urging them to go on offense and fight back boldly and vocally against this extremism. If they do, our testing shows, they can shift their races 4 to 5 points in their favor. To put this in perspective, a shift that big in 2024 would have meant a 57-seat Republican Senate majority — or, in the other direction, President Kamala Harris and a Democrat-controlled House.

Democrats are vulnerable on this issue. Their pollsters and strategists know it, advising them to keep their position vague. Several Massachusetts House Democrats broke ranks and criticized the new law . More often, like Kamala Harris in 2024, they flat-out deny that elective late-term abortions happen .

These denials get less plausible all the time. By our count, Massachusetts as joined the District of Columbia and 11 other states in having no gestational limits whatsoever on abortion — a strange growth for something that supposedly never happens. In reality, the data say that abortions in America are overwhelmingly done for elective or unspecified reasons, no matter at what point in pregnancy.

In another striking example, Ohio’s U.S. Senate candidate Sherrod Brown now counts retired late-term abortionist Warren Hern as a campaign donor . Hern, who isn’t media-shy, views every pregnancy as a “medical problem .” He admits to performing sex-selection abortions and estimates that at least half of abortions at his center involved healthy mothers and healthy babies.

Like almost every other Senate and House Democrat, Brown co-sponsored legislation to turn Warren Hern’s and Massachusetts’ policy of nine-month abortions into a national mandate, forcing all 50 states to allow elective late-term abortion, paid for by taxpayers. In this year’s intense battlegrounds across the country, many ostensibly moderate Democrats are on the record supporting similar or identical laws.

Most voters need no convincing that late-term abortion in the seventh, eighth, and ninth month of pregnancy — when the baby can suck her thumb, recognize mom or dad’s voice, feel pain, and survive outside the womb with care — is abhorrent. The overwhelming constant, before and after Dobbs , is that about seven in 10 Americans reject the no-limits Democratic Party position. Even rank-and-file Democrats are less enthusiastic about abortion since Dobbs .

Nor are Americans inherently opposed to limits on late-term abortions at the national level, with exceptions, especially contrasted with the Democrats’ all-trimester legal abortion mandate. Few would even consider this a “ban,” in the Democrats’ poll-tested terms. In many cases they simply haven’t heard the argument yet.

But hear it they must. What happens in Massachusetts is not just a Massachusetts problem, it is a preview of what is coming everywhere under a future Democratic trifecta. The bill is written, sponsored, voted on, promised, and Democrats will not hesitate to eliminate the Senate filibuster to pass it.

Some on the right voice skepticism that the issue of protecting human life can get enough people to the polls, in an election dominated by concerns about affordability, healthcare, Iran and more. No one expects candidates to stop talking about these topics, of course. But the first thing to remember is that Republicans cannot win without their base.

That base is indeed passionately pro-life and expects Republicans to address more than 1.1 million lives cruelly ended each year in America. Otherwise, there will be attrition of the most engaged voters and volunteers .

Democrats have not called a truce, either. The fallacy is that the “ostrich strategy” of avoiding the abortion question on the campaign trail and just hoping to survive until it goes away is a winning plan.

Pro-life Republicans must fearlessly call out their opponents on their extremism. They must run toward the battle, not away from it. The people will stand with them.

With our help and the Democrats’ miscalculations, the tools they need to win the abortion battle are within their reach.

Marjorie Dannenfelser is president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America.

articles.body:
▪ Investigation launched into Amazon plane crash

President Trump predicted in a Labor Day message on Truth Social that Republicans would win “big” on Election Day. But Republicans are facing stiffening economic headwinds as election season kicks into high gear.

A record was set Monday as the average cost of a gallon of regular gas was above $4 on Labor Day for the first time ever. AAA recorded the price at $4.15 per gallon, more than 30 cents higher than the previous record of $3.82, set in 2012.

This came after the average price of diesel hit a new high Friday, a mark that was surpassed each day of the weekend .

AAA noted in its analysis that gas prices typically drop this time of year because of reduced demand, but the high cost of crude oil is keeping them elevated.

The soaring cost of energy has also fueled overall inflation, which ticked up to 3.4 percent year-over-year, according to last month’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) — well above the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent target and slightly higher than former President Biden ’s final months in office. Economists and politicians alike will be keeping a close eye on the new CPI numbers coming this week.

Costs on some goods are set to rise further after Canada’s 50 percent retaliatory tariffs took effect at midnight . Canadian officials have vowed to meet Trump’s 50 percent tariffs “dollar for dollar,” escalating the trade war between the two countries and posing a particular challenge for GOP candidates in border battleground races.

There’s also continued volatility in the global bond markets, a key indicator of economic anxiety, with yields ticking up at the start of the week.

The economic picture isn’t all bad news for Trump and his party.

The job market has continued to prove its resilience despite economic uncertainty. The economy added 162,000 jobs in August, well above the 53,000 that had been expected, as the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1 percent.

That is a key victory that Trump and congressional GOP candidates can tout on the campaign trail as part of their message that the economy is strong despite the high costs.

But these numbers also mean the Federal Reserve is more likely to raise interest rates, an idea that would be anathema to Trump, who has repeatedly called on the Fed to be more aggressive in lowering rates. The Hill’s Julia Shapero reports that the latest job numbers alleviate concerns that the higher rates are weakening the labor market, allowing the Fed to focus more on curtailing inflation.

The Fed has kept interest rates steady over its past five meetings, but traders are pricing a roughly 60 percent chance that the agency increases rates by a quarter point at its next meeting later this month.

That would be unwelcome, and untimely, news for Republicans. Still, the main driver of economic anxiety continues to be the Iran war.

The U.S. has touted its growing control over the Strait of Hormuz, which has allowed a steady, if limited, flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. Iran appears determined to change these dynamics.

Mohsen Rezaei , the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Iranian state-run media on Sunday that Tehran plans to announce a “restricted zone” by the strait in the coming days. Under the plan, any ship that enters the area with the intention of passing through the strait will be placed on a sanctions list and face “consequences.”

Rezaei said the zone will cover the region within the U.S. Navy’s blockade, extend toward the strait and continue into the Persian Gulf.

The escalation follows the latest round of tit-for-tat strikes between the U.S. and Iran since negotiations to reach a resolution to the conflict fell apart last month. U.S. Central Command hit three Iranian oil tankers located near Kharg Island and the Gulf of Oman on Saturday in response to Iranian attacks on U.S. Navy warships.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday that about two-thirds of the daily traffic that the strait had before the war is getting through.

The administration has also been touting the deal it made with Venezuela to gain control of 65 billion barrels of the country’s oil to help provide relief to consumers. But experts have signaled time may be needed before any impacts could be felt.

Despite these developments, the cost of crude oil has been back on the rise in recent weeks, inching past $90 per barrel .

That will give Democrats a powerful cudgel as candidates and political parties ramp up advertising, campaign stops and debates in the weeks ahead.

‘UTTER DEVASTATION’ : An investigation is underway after five people were killed and five others were injured when an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday.

Three of the injured people were in critical condition, while two were hospitalized with less severe injuries.

The National Transportation Safety Board said it is sending a team to Miami led by the agency’s chair, Jennifer Homendy , to conduct the investigation. She said Monday that all five people killed were inside a van, which was carrying seven people from a cleaning company, or an SUV that were outside of airport property.

She called the scene at the crash “utter devastation.”

The flight was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, when it overran the runway around 2 p.m. and continued across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses surrounding the airport. The plane burst into flames upon impact, and more than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the crash.

The Associated Press reported that federal investigators are likely to focus on whether the plane touched down too late to stop safely. Video of the landing appears to show the plane passing over a significant portion of the runway before touching down.

Experts told the outlet that the typical landing zone for a plane is within the first 3,000 feet of a runway, and if the plane was beyond that area, it should have aborted the landing.

The Miami airport isn’t equipped with lightweight, crushable material that’s been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that go past the end of a runway, AP reported.

CROWDED FIELD : Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth may have a favorite to lead the Army following Dan Driscoll ’s resignation last week, but his pick has some other notable competition.

Sources familiar with the process told The Hill’s Filip Timotija that Hegseth’s choice, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell , is one of at least four candidates being considered for Army secretary. Others in consideration include at least two current officials — Marc Andersen , an assistant secretary of the Army, and Derrick Anderson , an assistant secretary of defense.

Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.), the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and an Army veteran, is also in the field.

Trump has chosen Adam Telle , the assistant secretary of the Army for civil works, as the acting Army secretary , a move that Timotija reports caught some current officials by surprise. When Trump will nominate a permanent replacement to Driscoll or whether Telle will serve in the role for the long term is unclear.

“Every senior leader in [the] Pentagon knows that Secretary Hegseth’s preferred pick is Sean Parnell,” a senior Pentagon official said. “Sean’s well-respected across the Department, and viewed as a solid choice.”

Parnell previously ran for Senate in Pennsylvania with Trump’s support but withdrew from the race in November 2021 after losing a court battle over custody of his children. FIGHTING ON : German Chancellor Friedrich Merz vowed to plow ahead with the country’s democratic values and firm stance against Russia after a far-right party won a major victory in a state election for the first time since the Nazi era.

Merz acknowledged that the victory for the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt was “the most serious election defeat” that his own center-right Christian Democratic Union suffered in years. But he said he would remain as the leader of Germany, as “giving up is not an option for me.”

AfD, a party whose regional branch in Saxony-Anhalt is considered a right-wing extremist group by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, finished well ahead of the other parties in the regional election Sunday. It fell just short of a majority and may need partners from other parties to form a governing coalition.

That would normally be difficult, as Germany’s mainstream parties have refused to work with AfD as part of a so-called “firewall” to prevent the party from gaining power. But AfD is only three seats short of a majority and may reach out to the far-left BSW party.

Despite being on opposing sides of the political spectrum, AfD and BSW both share anti-immigration and Russia-friendly sentiments.

That could pave the way for AfD’s candidate, Ulrich Siegmund , to become governor of the state.

Merz doubled down on economic reforms that he says are necessary to get Germany’s sluggish economy going despite their unpopularity. Still, he said officials must do better to justify the reforms, including to the country’s pension system, “not just rationally but also emotionally.”

And finally … The late actor Rob Reiner received a posthumous Emmy Award over the weekend for his guest appearance on FX’s “The Bear” before his death.

Reiner won the award for outstanding guest actor in a comedy as part of the ceremony for awards given out a week before the main Emmys ceremony, which is set to air on Sept. 14. He appeared in three episodes of the show that aired last year.

Deadline reported that Wendy McLendon-Covey , who presented the award, accepted it on his behalf , saying “We all wish he was here” as the audience gave a standing ovation.

Reiner and his wife, photographer Michele Singer , were found dead in December at their home in Los Angeles. Their son, Nick Reiner , is facing two counts of first-degree murder. He has pleaded not guilty.

Rob Reiner is the first posthumous winner of an Emmy in an acting category since Raul Julia , who won for “The Burning Season” in 1995 following his death the prior year, CNN reported .
